doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Defining improvisation: the flutaphone girl
summary: Rowe asks if improvisation must be jazz; Jordan tells of a shy girl on flutaphone who improvised once she began.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we’re in Rome, New York filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m really privileged to have Edward “Kidd” Jordan with me today, saxophonist, educator, composer and constant improviser. You were just telling me about your definition of improvisation. Is it something that has to be jazz music?

No. In fact, I had a little girl, one time I was teaching a class like this. And we had a flutaphone player, and a little girl, we had about three or four of them. You know they’re limited. And she was very shy about playing. But when she got started she started improvising of those four or five notes, and I had to just say, “you got it.” I mean she played so much after she got started and got it up, and she really was improvising and I mean it was serious. She didn’t have any idea about notes or changes or whatever, she was just learning the key — the system of the flutaphone. But when she got started she got all the harmonics out, and the way she was, you know, fingers in different positions. It really was something marvelous to behold.
